newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-ROME 2004 BID PRAISED FOR SECURITY PLANS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ROME 2004 BID PRAISED FOR SECURITY PLANS.

text.p: An International Olympic Committee (IOC) commission evaluating the bids for the 2004 Summer Games on Saturday praised Rome for its security plans, its professionalism and proposed athletes' village.

Commission president Thomas Bach, a 42-year-old German lawyer who won an Olympic team fencing gold medal at the 1976 Montreal Games, singled out "three strong impressions" at a news conference closing the visit to Rome.
He said the first point was that the IOC commission felt they had been met in Italy by "a very well-prepared team that worked in a most professional manner".
"It clearly demonstrated close cooperation between all the parties concerned," he said.

Bach said the second impression was of "thorough and detailed planning of the Olympic village in Tor Vergata. We appreciated the consultation of five Italian Olympic champions to ensure the interest of athletes are well taken care of."
The third point, a major worry for a city hit in the past by violence involving Middle Eastern groups and guerrillas, concerned security matters during the Games.
Bach, flanked by two of Italy's three IOC members and mayor of Rome Francesco Rutelli, reassured the city.
"The commission feels very confident of the security plans of the candidate city," he said, saying that they were shown a "very deep analysis of the security implications".
"The already tried and tested cooperation between security and sports movements gives a feeling of general confidence to the whole Olympic family," Bach said.
Rome hosted the 1960 Olympics, before the innocence of the modern Games was shattered by the massacre of Israeli athletes by Palestinian guerrillas at the 1972 Munich Games.
The city, which intends to use renovated but existing sports facilities for the 2004 Games, has also hosted the 1990 World Cup soccer final and other major sporting events.

Bach said a bombing at this year's Atlanta Summer Games, which killed two people, had not changed the evaluation process. "It's not a lesson we had to learn from recent times. We have always had it in mind," he said.
The German said the points had been voted on by his members and would be reflected in their final report to the IOC.
On February 28 next year, the commission is due to release its report. A short-list of four or five cities will be selected at the end of March and the winner announced in September.
The other cities are: Cape Town, Buenos Aires, Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Stockholm, Seville, Athens and St Petersburg.
Asked whether any negative points had emerged in Rome, Bach replied that if there were he would not reveal them.
"I never saw Primo so happy, so don't spoil his afternoon," he said, referring to International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) head and IOC member Primo Nebiolo.
Nebiolo had said earlier that Bach's three impressions were "excellent, excellent, excellent" for Rome's bid.
